extracted.intended_audience: patent practitioners, inventors, law students, and judges evaluating patent specifications
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and legal standards for preparing and evaluating a patent specification: sufficiency/enablement, disclosure of best mode/materials, drawings, formalities, and statutory amendment/disclaimer procedures. Focuses on what a specification must disclose so a person of ordinary skill can practice the invention.

rubrics_metrics.name: Specification sufficiency / enablement
rubrics_metrics.description: The specification must describe the invention sufficiently so that a person of ordinary and competent skill can make and use it without having to exercise inventive skill or to set themselves a problem to solve.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: As stated: 'If ... engineers of ordinary and competent skill would have to set themselves a problem to solve, and would have to solve that problem before they could do it, then the specification would be bad.' The sufficiency question is generally one of fact for a jury/expert evidence. Examples and case law (e.g., Neilson v. Harford) illustrate that if a workman of ordinary skill can, from the specification alone, construct an apparatus productive of some beneficial result, the specification will be sufficient.

rubrics_metrics.name: Measured against a person of ordinary skill (not an expert)
rubrics_metrics.description: The specification is to be judged by whether a practical workman of ordinary skill and ordinary knowledge in the subject could understand and apply it, not by whether a first-rate or highly scientific person could make further inventions from a mere hint.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Quoted guidance: 'it is supposed to be addressed to a practical workman, who brings the ordinary degree of knowledge and the ordinary degree of capacity to the subject.' Do not require extraordinary scientific knowledge when testing sufficiency.

rubrics_metrics.name: Disclosure of the best mode / most advantageous method/materials
rubrics_metrics.description: The patentee is bound to give the most advantageous mode known to him and any circumstance conducive to the advantageous operation of the invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Omission of a mode or circumstance the inventor knew to be advantageous can vitiate the patent: e.g., failing to state use of tallow, aqua-fortis, or other facilitating materials has been held fatal. The patentee 'does not pay the price for his monopoly' if he withholds knowledge that would make the invention work better.

rubrics_metrics.name: No omission of materially advantageous details
rubrics_metrics.description: If anything is omitted which gives an advantageous operation to the thing invented, that omission will vitiate the patent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Concrete anti-patterns: listing ingredients without proportions in a composition; failing to mention a material or use the patentee actually used when that use materially affects the operation. Courts will treat such omissions as rendering the specification defective.

rubrics_metrics.name: Disclosure of material condition and purity (foreign matter)
rubrics_metrics.description: If the specification directs the use of a substance which generally contains foreign matter that is positively injurious, and does not show any method of removing that foreign matter or how to procure the substance in a proper state, the specification will be defective.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: using a raw material that ordinarily contains harmful impurities without explaining how to make it suitable or where to obtain a proper form will render the disclosure insufficient.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identify procurement/source when common name is ambiguous
rubrics_metrics.description: If an article is described by a particular name but the patentee knows the requisite article cannot ordinarily be procured under that name, and does not state where it may be procured, the specification is defective because the public lacks full and precise information.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When commodity names are ambiguous in the relevant market, specify source, state of preparation, or means of obtaining the correct material to enable practice by skilled persons.

rubrics_metrics.name: Must distinguish the improvement from prior modes
rubrics_metrics.description: Where the manner of applying power or effect varies with circumstances, the specification must show in what the improvement consists, as distinguished from all former modes of doing the same thing, otherwise it will be defective.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The disclosure should explain the inventive contribution relative to prior art rather than merely describing variable application without clarifying the novel principle or effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: No concealment via obscure terms or misleading statements
rubrics_metrics.description: A specification using obscure terms for the sake of concealment, or making misleading statements (e.g., claiming a preference for a material while concealing that no other will answer), is bad.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid intentionally opaque language or misstatements that would induce belief that elaborate processes are necessary when simple ones suffice; such conduct misleads the public and risks invalidity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Compositions — proportions and vagueness rule
rubrics_metrics.description: For compositions of matter, if the specification is so drawn that no one can use the invention without ascertaining by experiment the exact proportions required, the patent will be void; however, a general rule proportion with variable exceptions applicable to varying states of ingredients is permissible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts allow a stated general proportion (a 'general rule') and permit variable exceptions for different ingredient states; whether the rule is 'susceptible of application' and furnishes means to determine specific proportions is a factual question for the jury or experts. Absolute vagueness (only listing ingredients with no proportions) is fatal.

rubrics_metrics.name: No need to describe ordinary or known processes/terms
rubrics_metrics.description: The specification need not describe processes, apparatus, or terms that are within the ordinary knowledge of the workman to whom the specification is addressed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Technical knowledge is presumed for the skilled addressee; a specification using scientific terms that are understood by those in the art is acceptable even if an ordinary person would not understand them. Known components need not be re-explained.

rubrics_metrics.name: Suggest necessary particular knowledge/steps when not common
rubrics_metrics.description: If the practical application involves a particular kind of knowledge requiring the workman to do something not within ordinary practice, the specification must at least suggest to him that that thing is to be done (even if it does not fully teach how).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If an aspect requires special technical problem-solving, the specification should point to that problem or method so the skilled person knows to apply that knowledge rather than leaving it entirely unstated.

rubrics_metrics.name: Specify materials when choice is essential
rubrics_metrics.description: It is not necessary to state of what material every part should be made when the principle and effect are the same across materials; but if a particular material is essential to the successful operation, the patentee must direct the use of that material.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Indicate materials explicitly when the invention's function depends on them; otherwise omitting non-essential material details is acceptable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Drawings as part of the specification
rubrics_metrics.description: Where the nature of the case admits of drawings, the statute directs the patentee to accompany the specification with drawings and written references; drawings annexed constitute part of the specification and may be used to explain or help out an otherwise imperfect written description.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A specification may be partly in writing and partly in drawing; the combination must enable a skilled mechanic to perform the work and show what is claimed. Written description need not always reference the drawing explicitly if both together enable understanding.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scale of drawings not required unless necessary
rubrics_metrics.description: Although drawings were once required to be on a scale, the rule is modified: if a mechanic can make the subject from a perspective drawing, a scale is not necessary; but if the subject could not be made without many experiments unless the drawing is to scale, the specification (writing+drawing) is defective.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use scale when dimensional proportions are critical to practice; otherwise perspective or non-scaled drawings are acceptable so long as the combination with text enables practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Formal attestation/signature requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: The statute requires formal attestation: the specification and drawings must be signed by the inventor and attested by two witnesses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure signatures and witness attestations are provided per statutory formalities; there is some uncertainty in the case law whether both specification and drawings must be separately signed, but signing the specification that refers to drawings effectively attests them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Amendment to add improvements after issuance
rubrics_metrics.description: Provision exists (Act of 1836 §13) for amendment of the specification by filing descriptions of new improvements made after the patent has issued; the commissioner annexes them with a certificate of filing and they thereafter have the same effect as if embraced in the original specification.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To preserve later improvements, file an amendment per statutory procedure and obtain the certificate; the added description becomes part of the specification as of filing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Disclaimer procedure for overbroad claims
rubrics_metrics.description: Where, through inadvertence, accident, or mistake, the patentee has made his specification or claim too broad (claiming more than he was the original inventor of), the patentee may file a disclaimer of the parts not claimed to be held, stating extent of interest; disclaimer must be in writing, attested, recorded in the Patent Office, and accompanied by payment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The disclaimer operates as part of the original specification as to the interest retained; filing affects pending suits differently depending on timing (see next item). Filing a disclaimer does not affect suits pending at filing except as to unreasonable neglect/delay.

rubrics_metrics.name: Statutory protection for inadvertent overclaiming (§9 of 1837 act) and cost limitations
rubrics_metrics.description: If a patentee by mistake claimed as original what he was not the original inventor of, the patent is deemed valid for so much as is truly and bona fide his own; the patentee may maintain suit for that part, but to recover costs he must have entered at the Patent Office a disclaimer of the part claimed without right and must not have unreasonably neglected to do so.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This provides a remedy rather than an outright invalidation for inadvertent overclaiming, but imposes procedural requirements (disclaimer filing) to obtain full benefits like costs. Courts will bar costs if disclaimer not timely filed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Timing effect of disclaimers on suits
rubrics_metrics.description: The disclaimer under the seventh section applies to suits pending when the disclaimer was filed; the disclaimer under the ninth section applies to suits brought after the disclaimer is filed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be mindful of the timing of filing a disclaimer relative to litigation; statutory distinctions affect remedy, applicability, and recovery of costs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Specification invalidated by materially untrue statements that would mislead a competent workman
rubrics_metrics.description: If the specification contains an untrue statement in a material circumstance that, if literally acted upon by a competent workman, would mislead him and cause the experiment to fail, the specification is bad and the patent invalidated—even if a competent workman could correct the error in practice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Material falsity that would cause failure of practice is fatal. Courts may nonetheless consider whether skilled persons would be misled; but literal reliance on a materially false statement that would cause failure is sufficient to invalidate.
